findings.title: The code images still hold the fixes in their git history
body: The paper says Xiaomi kept each repository's history only up to the task's base commit, and removed build outputs that could reveal the fix. The released images do not match that.

In the images with the repository in /testbed, the builders cloned the upstream project and reset it to the base commit. The later commits are still in git's object store, and the branch reflog still points at the upstream tip, so git log --reflog shows them. In the images with the repository in /workspace/repo, the upstream branches and tags were never removed, so git diff HEAD main shows the removed code.

We checked 16 code images, and all 16 let an agent read commits from after the base. In the 6 we inspected closely, the exact fix was there every time. In the Astro task, git log --reflog --grep trailingslash finds the upstream fix, and applying it makes the hidden tests pass. Two images also hold compiled copies of the fixed code, e.g., a Java class file with the method the task asks for.

Xiaomi's released harness checks for leftover history, but only through branches and tags. So it refuses to start the /workspace/repo tasks, and it does not notice the reflog leaks in the /testbed tasks. Its git_leak_prevention: strip option should fix the git part, but it is off by default for this dataset.

findings.title: 25 general tasks cannot reach full reward as released
body: The code checks in 51 general tasks compare the database after the run with a copy called state.db.pinned_backup. That file is not in the release, and Xiaomi's released harness never creates it.

When the file is missing, sqlite opens a new empty database, so the check crashes and the item scores 0. We ran every check twice on the untouched environment, once as released and once with the backup added.

In 28 tasks, 43 rubric items fail only because the backup is missing (11 of them are critical). 25 of these tasks can no longer reach a reward of 1.0. Their median best possible reward is 0.75, and the lowest is 0.40.
The fix is one line in the harness: copy each state.db to state.db.pinned_backup before the agent starts.

findings.title: 278 cyber training tasks are CyberGym test bugs
body: Both sets come from ARVO, a public set of reproducible OSS-Fuzz bugs. 135 cyber training tasks have the same ARVO id as a CyberGym task. 139 more are the same bug under a new number. OSS-Fuzz renumbered all its issues in 2024, and the training set uses the new numbers while CyberGym uses the old ones. 4 more share an OSS-Fuzz id with CyberGym's own oss-fuzz tasks.

In all, 278 of the 1,000 training tasks match 223 CyberGym tasks, which is 15% of the benchmark. For 269 of them, CyberGym's own crash report names the same bug type and function as the training task.

The paper reports CyberGym scores of 94.0 for Pro and 95.1 for Flash. 102 of the overlapping training tasks also match 82 ExploitGym tasks, another benchmark in the paper. The paper does not say whether it removed these bugs from its evaluation, and we cannot tell whether these tasks were in the Pro and Flash runs. Anyone comparing CyberGym scores should drop these bugs.

findings.title: The music reward never checks the prompt
body: Every music prompt asks for a key, a tempo, a meter, instruments, a number of voices and a length.

Xiaomi's released scorer converts the ABC notation to MIDI and scores how close 18 statistics of the notes are to human music. It does not read the prompt. The code says so: "the scorer looks only at the ABC the policy emitted", and grading instruction-following is something "this scorer does not do".

We scored pieces with the unmodified scorer. Six pieces Claude wrote to follow their prompts scored 0.60 to 0.89. A piece of uniformly random chromatic notes, split into a treble and a bass voice, scored 0.77, higher than five of the six. One C major chord repeated for 64 bars scored 0.49. Our own random pieces without the treble and bass split scored about 0.65.

So a model can ignore the request and still earn most of the reward. Formatting matters much more: one blank line inside the notation, or a sentence of text after it, drops the reward to 0. The dataset card lists the music grader as rule checks, which is easy to read as checking the request.

findings.title: Some environments cannot be graded offline as released
body: The paper says containers have no network. In 2 of the 6 code images we inspected, the hidden tests cannot run without it. The jcabi-github image has no local Maven repository, so Maven needs to download packages. In the go-lark image, Go looks for modules in the wrong folder, because the images were flattened into one layer without their environment variables, e.g., GOPATH.
One of the two terminal images we checked is missing two Python packages, so its vendored library cannot even be imported, and a correct fix cannot pass offline.

findings.title: 172 general tasks give reward to an agent that does nothing
body: We ran every code check in the 925 general tasks against a fresh copy of each task's databases and files, with Xiaomi's own released grader function. We gave no final answer, so every LLM item scored 0.
172 tasks still paid out a reward above zero. The average free reward in those tasks is 0.26. It is at least 0.2 in 126 tasks and at least 0.5 in 15.

Most of it comes from sanity and do-no-harm items, which check that the agent did not break anything. They are meant to pass when nothing changes, so that damage costs reward. But because they carry the same weight as the real items, a do-nothing rollout starts well above zero, and the reward range left for doing the task is smaller.
If the missing backup files were present, as Xiaomi's pipeline seems to expect, 193 tasks would pay out free reward.

findings.title: In 30 general tasks, a critical check passes before the agent starts
body: Some tasks ask the agent to create or update a record, but the starting database already holds the right values for part of it.

Task s3k_0117 asks the agent to give an inventory investigation the right owner, cause, signed adjustment and open status. The untouched database already has the correct cause code, the correct adjustment of -5,500,000 cents and the correct links. So 3 of the 5 critical checks pass with no action. Only the owner and the status need to change.

30 tasks have at least one critical code check that passes on the untouched environment. Some of these are do-no-harm checks labeled critical. Others, like this example, check values the task asks the agent to produce.

findings.title: The 1,000 cyber tasks are only 836 distinct bugs
body: 164 bugs appear twice in the training set, once under the old OSS-Fuzz number and once under the new one. Each copy has its own Docker image, and 163 of the 164 pairs have word for word the same target. Rows 0 and 221 are the same dnsmasq bug.

26 tasks target an abort in LLVMFuzzerInitialize, the function that sets up the fuzzer before it reads any input. So any input may trigger it. We did not run the cyber tasks, so we could not confirm this.

findings.title: 74 website prompts refer to an image the dataset does not include
body: 74 website prompts ask the agent to use an attached file, e.g., "use the attached screenshot as the main visual reference" or "use the attached mockup/logo for style reference".
Every row in the dataset is text only, and the webdev Docker image has no per-task files either. So the agent never sees the file, and the grader cannot check whether the site follows it.

findings.title: Some rubric weights are set in ways the grader ignores
body: The grader reads each item's weight from a field called weight, and uses 1 when the field is missing.
9 items put their weight in a field called points or rubric_weight instead, so the grader ignores it.

In 9 tasks, some items have weights written as fractions that add up to 1, while other items have no weight and count as 1 each. In s3k_0000, five LLM items have weights that add up to 1.0, and one sanity check has no weight, so it counts as another 1.0. That check passes on the untouched environment, so doing nothing earns 0.5.
One LLM item has no question at all, so the judge sees only the expected answer.

findings.title: 481 music prompts state a length that does not match their tempo
body: The prompts come from two fixed templates, and the stated length depends only on the bar count. It ignores the tempo and the meter. Row 291 asks for 64 bars of 2/4 at 172 BPM, which lasts under a minute, and calls it "about three minutes". 481 of the 1,000 prompts state a length more than 25% off from bars times beats per bar divided by BPM.

Other template slips: 16 English prompts ask for a piece "in 1 voices" and then ask to "thin the middle section to two voices". 72 prompts ask to open with the whole ensemble "alone, then layer the other parts in one at a time". 48 say things like "a organ prelude". The scorer never reads the prompt, so none of this changes the reward, but a model trained on these prompts learns to read past contradictions.

findings.title: 41 website prompts still start with the word "Prompt:"
body: These prompts begin with "Prompt:" or "PROMPT:", which looks like a label left over from the step that generated them. It is harmless, but it shows the prompts are synthetic and were not cleaned by hand.

findings.title: Every row says the reward style is "rule"
body: The reward_model.style field is "rule" in all 7,780 rows, including the 3,018 general and webdev tasks that an LLM or a vision model grades. The ground_truth field is empty in every row. So you cannot tell from the rows how a task is graded, or what the answer is.

findings.title: The five configs do not share one schema
body: The cyber file has no ability column. The music file has no agent_name column and no instance_json, and keeps its fields in extra_info instead. Column order and string types also differ between files. Code that loads all five configs has to handle each one separately.

findings.title: 10 general tasks ship stale database backups
body: These tasks have files such as state.db.pre_fix_backup, state.db.repair_backup and state.db.before_fill next to the real database. They sit in the sidecar folder, so the agent cannot read them. They show that some databases were patched after they were generated, and they add clutter.

findings.title: The released grader falls back to gpt-4o-mini as the judge
body: The general verifier reads its judge model from environment variables and uses gpt-4o-mini when none is set. The paper used Xiaomi's own MiMo-V2.6-SFT model as the judge. Rewards you get from the released code can differ from the ones used in training, depending on the judge you choose.

findings.title: Some code tests install packages while grading
body: 106 code tasks run npm install and 133 run pip install inside the test command. The paper says containers have no network access, to stop agents from downloading the fix. If grading also runs without the network, these installs only work when the packages are already cached in the image.

In our 8-task pilot this did not break grading. One test script fell back to yarn install and skipped it because the packages were already in the image. One project's own test runner tried to download a tool, but the hidden script calls pytest directly, which works offline.

findings.title: Claude solved 8 of the 8 code tasks we tried, and every task was valid
body: We ran Claude as the agent on 8 code tasks in their own Docker images, with the network off and without looking at the hidden tests. Graded the way Xiaomi's harness grades, which resets the test files and then applies the hidden patch, it solved all 8. In all 8 tasks the hidden tests fail on the untouched repository, so none gives free reward.

The run also turned up small problems. In one task the hidden test calls a method named Core that the prompt never mentions. In two tasks the image already has the new npm packages that the reference fix adds. One task's existing end-to-end tests describe the feature the agent must restore. One prompt describes a crash that the original code already catches.
This is a small, hand-picked sample, with a different harness from Xiaomi's, so it says little about difficulty.

findings.title: The release covers part of the paper's RL mix
body: The paper's RL data was 68% coding, 13% design, 12% general tool use, 4% cyber and 3% context following. The release has no competitive coding and no context following tasks. The paper's visual tasks include games, 3D scenes, slides, SVG, video and Figma designs, but every webdev task in the release is a website. The release also has no reference solutions, no rollouts and no pass rates.

findings.title: Where the code tasks come from
body: The code tasks fall into five groups by how they are packaged. The pathway names are our guesses at the paper's five sources. Group A (843) is pull requests whose issue text was rewritten by an LLM. Group B (606) uses GitHub issues as written, and 596 of them match a real issue title and body. Group C (454) is detailed written specifications. Group D (276) is employee-style requests with old and new test modes, some partly in Chinese. Group E (519) has first-person "I want" requests with black-box tests, which looks like the paper's CodeMidas pathway, where a feature is removed from a repository.

159 tasks are the same task as a row in a public dataset, e.g., SWE-rebench. We could guess the repository for 1,376 tasks with high or medium confidence, and they come from 957 different repositories. The most common is pandas, with 33 tasks.
No code task comes from a SWE-bench Verified or SWE-bench Pro repository, and none matches a DeepSWE v1.1 task, which is the main code benchmark in the paper.

findings.title: The terminal tasks do not copy Terminal-Bench
body: We compared the 64 terminal tasks with Terminal-Bench 1.0 through 4.0 and two related task sets. No task is an exact or near copy, and none shares even one 8-word run of text with a Terminal-Bench task. All 64 are one kind of task: repair a bug in a frozen copy of a library.

tastes.name: One mixed run per model
body: Each model got a single RL run of 30 steps that mixed coding, office work, design, context following and cyber in every batch. Most open RL work trains one domain at a time, because tasks with very different lengths and pass rates make a batch unstable.
They built a Sample Mixer to keep each source's share of the batch steady, even though rollout times differ 66 times between sources.

tastes.name: Small custom harnesses, with the real ones held out
body: They do not train inside Claude Code or Codex. They built four tiny agent loops and vary the harness on purpose, as a third kind of diversity next to tasks and environments. The real harnesses are kept for evaluation only.
On DeepSWE, the average score across the three held-out harnesses rose from about 50% to 66% during training.
tastes.quote: These extras fall outside the task-completion reward signal, making credit assignment unreliable

tastes.name: Grading is a budget line
body: For MiMo-V2.6-Pro, 12.7% of the $2.6M RL cost went to grading, next to 43.8% for rollouts and 43.5% for training. The graders are agents that open the environment and read the trajectories, not a single test result.
tastes.quote: rollout consumes 43.8% and training 43.5%, while the grader takes the remaining 12.7%

tastes.name: Reward as a product, so tests stay in charge
body: For code tasks that most rollouts pass, an agent writes task-specific rubrics from earlier attempts. The reward is the test result times a solution score times a behavior score.
A failed test always gives zero, so a good rubric score can never rescue a wrong patch. But passing patches still get different rewards, so even a group where everything passes teaches something.

tastes.name: Rank the passing patches, keep the total the same
body: For other code tasks, an agent grader reads all 16 rollouts together and ranks the passing patches on approach, precision, minimality, side effects and craft. Advantage moves from weak passes to strong ones, while the total advantage of the passing rollouts stays the same.
Without this, the paper says policies drifted toward speculative compatibility branches, swallowed exceptions and relaxed validation to pass tests.
tastes.quote: it redistributes positive advantage mass from lower-quality to higher-quality successful trajectories

tastes.name: An infrastructure failure never counts as a zero
body: When a pod fails to start, a judge times out or a grader crashes, the rollout gets no reward at all instead of a zero, because a zero would teach the model that the failure was its fault.
In the webdev grader, a broken row gets the group's mean reward. Since GRPO only sees reward minus the group mean, that row then adds nothing to the gradient, with no change to the trainer.
tastes.quote: writing the mean gives exactly what a sentinel buys -- the row contributes no gradient -- without a trainer change

tastes.name: One report defines both the task and the grade
body: Each cyber task comes from one sanitizer report. The task text names the bug type and the function, and the grader compares exactly those two strings. The agent also gets the compiled program, not just the source code.
The paper argues CyberGym's rule, which compares the old and fixed programs, can reward the wrong crash, and that its LLM-written descriptions are often too vague.
tastes.quote: description and verification share a single source of truth

tastes.name: Reward music for being typical
body: The music scorer rewards a piece for sitting inside the middle 80% of human music on 18 statistics, such as rhythm, harmony and range. A piece that is extreme in any direction loses reward. Most quality rewards do the opposite and reward more of a good thing.
The same scorer does not check whether the piece follows the prompt. See the Issues page.
tastes.quote: Human-likeness scoring based on deviation from human music distributions.

tastes.name: Only penalize length once a prompt is solved
body: A successful rollout that is much longer than the group's shorter successful ones loses some reward. Failed rollouts are never penalized, and groups with a low pass rate are skipped, so hard prompts keep room to explore. The released config uses the 30th percentile of successful lengths as the reference, and a minimum pass rate of 0.5.
tastes.quote: the pass-rate gate preserves room for exploration on difficult prompts

tastes.name: Attack your own environments until nothing works
body: Before training, a hack agent probes every code environment for ways to cheat, using known leak routes as hints. They fix what it finds and run it again, until it finds nothing.

They also wrote mid-training examples in which MiMo notices its own reward-hacking reasoning, fixes that turn, and carries on with the real task. During training, confirmed hacks stayed under 2% of trajectories.
tastes.quote: We continued this process until the hack agent could no longer find a successful exploit in any of the environments.

tastes.name: Clean the git history down to the cruft packs
body: To stop agents from recovering the fix, they strip git history after the base commit and force garbage collection with cruft packs turned off, because a plain prune keeps recent unreachable objects for two weeks. Their anti-hack patterns came from 6,026 judged hacking trajectories.

tastes.name: A judge that can only say 0 or 1
body: In the office tasks, each rubric item is judged alone, and the judge must answer 0 or 1 with no partial credit. If the needed evidence was cut off, the answer is 0. If the judge cannot answer at all, the rollout is masked instead of scored.
Each item comes with a pass anchor that spells out the expected facts, which makes the judge's job close to a lookup.
tastes.quote: 只判 0 或 1,不给部分分 (only 0 or 1, no partial credit)

tastes.name: A broken page scores zero, not half
body: If a page's script fails to parse, throws on load or hangs the renderer, the reward is 0, not the visual score times a penalty. A penalty factor can be traded against looks, so the model would learn to accept broken pages that look good.
They also do not drop hung pages, because a dropped rollout gets zero advantage, which is better than a negative one. That would teach the model that hanging the renderer is safe.
tastes.quote: so RL treats a runtime error as a cost to amortise rather than a precondition

tastes.name: Remove the judge's position bias with a Latin square
body: The webdev judge compares all screenshots in a group. It runs 8 rounds with the screenshots in the order of a Williams Latin square, so each one appears in every position once. They measured that this cuts the first-position bias from about 0.28 votes to 0.03.
tastes.quote: measured to flatten the first-position bias from ±0.28 to ±0.03 votes

tastes.name: The agent physically cannot reach the database
body: In the office tasks, the mock software and its SQLite databases run in a separate sidecar container. The agent's container never mounts them, so the only way in is through the MCP tools. The answer keys are copied to the sidecar only at grading time.
tastes.quote: DB isolation is physical, so the agent cannot bypass the MCP tools with direct SQL

tastes.name: Freeze the MoE router
body: With a trainable router, expert load collapsed in the first 20 steps: the coefficient of variation rose from 0.78 to 2.0 and 22% of experts went cold. Resetting only the router to its pre-RL values fixed the balance without hurting scores, so they froze the router for RL.
tastes.quote: the collapse is driven by router drift rather than by degradation of the expert weights

tastes.name: Thresholds come from measured incidents
body: Many constants in the grader come with the incident behind them. 44 of 182 screenshots came back blank over the file protocol, so pages are served over http. The judge service collapses above about 1,000 concurrent calls, measured over 262,000 calls. The repetition threshold sits on a flat part of a measured two-peaked distribution.
tastes.quote: 0.15 is a plateau, not a tuned knob.

value.headline: About $1.4M to $1.9M at vendor prices
lead: We priced the dataset two ways: what a lab would pay vendors for similar tasks, and what it would cost to build them again. The middle cases land at $1.4M to $1.9M for vendor prices and about $2.0M to rebuild with pipelines.

The range is wide, from about $0.3M to $7.7M, because the market prices come from interviews rather than price lists. Almost all of the value sits in the 2,698 code tasks and the 989 general and terminal tasks.

assumptions: Vendor prices use Epoch AI's interviews with 18 people at environment startups and labs, who put most RL tasks at $200 to $2,000 each. We used $500 per task as the middle case for code, general and terminal tasks.

We lowered the vendor price because the release has no reference solutions, no rollouts and no pass rates. A buyer would need about 8 agent runs per task to recover pass rates and a working solution, and we added a 10% to 40% risk discount. The discount is our assumption.

The rebuild cost counts agent compute for validation, human review, and a few engineer-months to build each pipeline. Agent compute is small: 4 validation runs on every code task cost about $1K to $47K, depending on the model.
Cyber, webdev and music prices are our own assumptions, because we found no public prices for those kinds of tasks.
The Docker images add about 7.5 TB of storage. We did not price hosting.

about: We downloaded the five parquet files, the 925 general environment folders (without most workspace documents), and the image list from Hugging Face on 2026-09-26. We read the MiMo-V2.6 technical report and Xiaomi's verl fork at commit a2ad9f6.

We parsed every row to extract the fields you can filter by in the Tasks view. Languages come from langdetect. Test frameworks come from the test commands. Genres were translated from Chinese by hand. Docker image sizes come from the Docker Hub API.

For the general tasks we ran every code-based rubric check with Xiaomi's own released grader function on untouched copies of the databases, to measure the reward for doing nothing and to find checks that cannot pass.
The prompt map uses a multilingual static embedding model (model2vec potion-multilingual-128M) and UMAP.
We compared the cyber ids with CyberGym and the code problem statements with SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro.

Claude subagents helped: they read Xiaomi's training code for design choices, researched prices, composed music for the demo, inspected Docker images, and attempted 8 code tasks. We checked their key claims against the sources before using them.
caveats: We did not run the cyber tasks. Our attempt was stopped by Anthropic's cyber safety filters, so cyber findings are based on the data alone.
The code pilot is tiny and used a different agent and harness from Xiaomi's, so it says little about difficulty.
The released data is a subset of what the paper trained on, so findings about the release do not always apply to the paper's runs.
Value estimates rest on interview-based prices and our own assumptions. Treat them as a rough range.

pilot_code.notes: Added a dynamic-mapping entry to the ci schema and a handler in SpackCI.generate_ir that GETs <endpoint>?spec=<name@version variants arch=...%compiler> per build job, filters ignore/allow/require, warns 'Response missing required keys: [...]', deep-merges with merge_yaml, and warns on any request failure. Also added docs and my own tests (12 tests, local HTTP server). The hidden tests mock urllib.request.OpenerDirector.open, so any urllib-based client passes; they do not depend on private helper names. I recognized this as a real upstream Spack feature, so memory contamination is possible, but I did not reuse remembered helper names. By coincidence my own test file had the same path as the hidden test file (lib/spack/spack/test/cmd/ci_dynamic_mapping.py), so git apply refused the test patch; I deleted my file and re-applied. 2 of the 6 new hidden tests (schema rejection cases) pass even without a fix.
